item.title: BOJ declares inflation victory but still won't budge on rates, so what's the hold-up?
item.description:
If you think back to a decade ago, the BOJ being able to even see the path to reach the inflation target was very much a pipedream. Yet, here we are today. The central bank finally gets to declare victory on inflation. That must mean champagne all around, surely? Well, not quite.

As it would seem, getting to the finish line and convincing policymakers to do something about it are two very different things.

The BOJ kept its policy rate unchanged today at 1.25% in a 8-1 vote, with board member Takata dissenting in playing the role as the lone hawk again. He called for a 25 bps rate hike to 1.50% but the rest of the board wasn't having any of it. So, what's the story here?

The most interesting bit of the meeting decision today is that the BOJ now says that underlying inflation has reached a level broadly consistent with its 2% target. Policymakers also expect inflation to remain around there as we move forward. So, that is quite a milestone after more than a decade of trying to get inflation sustainably back on track.

Adding to that, the central bank also raised its core inflation forecast for fiscal year 2027 to 2.6% from 2.4% previously.

So if inflation is already where policymakers want it to be, what's stopping them from moving faster?

As it turns out, the overwhelming majority of the board clearly still prefers a more measured approach. Having just raised interest rates in September, there's little appetite to rush another move while assessing how previous tightening is feeding through to the economy. How typical of the BOJ, eh?

But in the bigger picture, I would argue that there is the political headache to consider.

Japan prime minister Takaichi's two board appointees, namely Asada and Sato, already voted against the rate hike in September. And that will serve as a reminder that getting further tightening through the board might not be quite so straightforward, even though the central bank has already declared victory on inflation.

Looking to next year, things could get even trickier and more challenging for the BOJ. Takaichi will have the opportunity to nominate replacements for two more board members in 2027. And if those appointments lean similarly dovish (which they likely will *coughs*), Ueda could find himself facing a more divided committee.

Even with today's signal, traders are pricing roughly 57% odds of another 25 bps rate hike in December. That is hardly a convincing endorsement of the next move, let alone any real confidence in the BOJ stepping up their tightening pace next year.

As for Ueda's press conference later, I would expect him to reiterate that further tightening remains on the table while keeping the timing deliberately vague. That'd be very on-brand of him. If anything, just watch for whether he puts more emphasis on the inflation milestone or the need to assess growth, wages and financial conditions.

But unless he offers something more definitive, I suspect markets will be left with much the same question heading into December.

After such a long battle, the BOJ has finally managed to tick the inflation box. However, now comes the harder part of getting everyone on board with what happens next.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

Co-founder Changpeng Zhao said the exchange appeared to have been hacked and that user funds were safe, and Binance pledged to cover all losses. It said about $2.5 billion has been frozen, but gave no figure for losses or a timeline for reopening.

Stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle moved quickly to freeze tokens linked to the outflows, acting within about 40 minutes of the drains beginning, according to reports. More than $1 billion, mostly ether, was reported to be beyond reach. Binance’s BNB token fell 8.6% to near $694 and bitcoin slipped to around $77,700.

item.title: BoJ declares underlying inflation at 2% target, lifts FY2027 price forecast as rates held
item.description:
The meeting delivered almost everything hawks had looked for: the 2% declaration, upside price risks, a higher inflation forecast and a dissent in favour of a hike, with no dovish split. That should support the yen near 157.8 per dollar, push short-dated JGB yields higher and firm December hike pricing from around 80%. Oil sits at the centre of the forecasts. The bank assumes Dubai crude falls from about $105 to $70, so a sustained rise in prices tied to the Iran conflict would add to the upside risk to inflation. Faster ETF sales add modest supply for Japanese equities from 2027, though a 43-year horizon keeps the annual impact small.

-The Bank of Japan has all but declared victory over deflation, and its own forecasts now say inflation is the bigger risk.

Summary:

  • , 0630 GMT,  in an 8-1 vote; Takata proposed a hike to 1.5%
  • The Outlook Report says underlying inflation is generally consistent with the 2% target and expected to stay there
  • Risks to prices are skewed to the upside, while risks to activity are generally balanced
  • FY2027 core CPI forecast raised to 2.6% from 2.4%; FY2026 unchanged at 2.5%, FY2028 at 2.0%
  • Real GDP is seen at 0.7% in FY2026 and FY2027 and 0.8% in FY2028
  • ETF sales will rise to about 860 billion yen a year from January 2027, cutting the disposal timeline to about 43 years from about 112

The Bank of Japan said underlying inflation is now generally consistent with its 2% price stability target, a long-awaited declaration that strengthens the case for further rate hikes. It kept its policy rate unchanged at 1.25% on Friday.

In its quarterly Outlook Report, the central bank said underlying consumer price inflation is at a level broadly in line with the target and is expected to stay around there. It pointed to a persistent sense of labour shortage, an interaction between rising wages and prices, and medium- to long-term inflation expectations of about 2%. The bank described the risks to prices as skewed to the upside. It warned that inflation expectations could rise and push underlying inflation above target as firms increasingly lift wages and prices.

The board’s median forecast for core inflation, which excludes fresh food, was raised to 2.6% for fiscal 2027 from 2.4% previously, reflecting the rise in crude oil prices since the summer. The fiscal 2026 forecast was unchanged at 2.5%, and fiscal 2028 stayed at 2.0%. The bank expects core inflation to rise to a level clearly above 2% in the first half of the projection period, driven by oil, higher prices for semiconductors and other items, and a weaker yen. It then sees inflation easing toward around 2% as the effect of high oil prices fades. Its projections assume Dubai crude falls from around $105 a barrel to around $70 by the end of the forecast period, and they exclude the effect of a proposed cut to the consumption tax on food.

Growth forecasts were little changed, with real GDP seen expanding 0.7% in fiscal 2026 and 2027 and 0.8% in fiscal 2028. The bank expects the economy to keep growing at a slower pace this fiscal year, as higher energy costs linked to the Middle East weigh on activity, supported by government measures and AI-related demand.

The policy board voted 8-1 to hold rates. Board member Hajime Takata dissented, proposing a hike to 1.5% on the grounds that with underlying inflation at target, the bank should speed up moves toward the neutral rate. No board member dissented in favour of a cut, removing a risk flagged ahead of the meeting.

The bank also unanimously agreed to more than double the pace of its ETF sales from January 2027, to about 860 billion yen a year on a book value basis from about 330 billion yen. That would shorten the time needed to sell its holdings to about 43 years from around 112.

Governor Kazuo Ueda’s press conference later on Friday, 0630 GMT,  will be watched for signals on whether the 2% declaration opens the door to a hike in December. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BoJ keeps policy rate unchanged at 1.25%, as expected
item.description:
BoJ keeps policy rate unchanged at 1.25%, as expected

The vote leans hawkish. The dissent the market feared, a call for a cut, didn’t happen, and the only objection came from a member pushing for a hike now. That should support the yen near 157.8 per dollar and keep December pricing, about 80% going in, firmly in place. Short-dated Japanese government bond yields may edge higher. The faster ETF sales add modest supply to Japanese equities from 2027, a mild headwind for the Nikkei. The final read will depend on the Outlook Report and Ueda’s tone, with oil-driven inflation pressure keeping the case for tightening alive.

---

  • BOJ preview: Daiwa sees hold, but 2% inflation call could open door to December hike
  • BoJ preview: MUFG sees hold but a 2% inflation call, with two dissenters the key yen risk
  • BOJ to hold at 1.25%, but Ueda signals further hikes toward neutral
  • BOJ seen lifting rates to 1.50% in December as 69% of economists expect a Q4 hike
  • BOJ reportedly may upgrade inflation forecast, hold rates steady at next week's meeting

---

The Bank of Japan stood still as expected, but the only voice of dissent wanted to go faster, and the yen bears’ nightmare of a dovish split never showed up.

Summary:

  • The BoJ held its short-term policy rate at around 1.25% in an 8-1 vote
  • Takata dissented, proposing a hike to 1.5% on the view that underlying inflation has reached the 2% target
  • No dovish dissent emerged, removing a key yen risk flagged before the meeting
  • The board unanimously raised the pace of ETF sales to about 860 billion yen a year (book value) from about 330 billion
  • The new ETF pace takes effect in January 2027; J-REIT sales are unchanged
  • Focus turns to the Outlook Report and Ueda’s press conference

The Bank of Japan kept its short-term policy rate unchanged at 1.25% on Friday, as widely expected. The decision came with a hawkish dissent and a sharp increase in the pace at which the central bank will sell its holdings of exchange-traded funds.

The policy board voted 8-1 to keep guiding the uncollateralised overnight call rate at around 1.25%. Board member Hajime Takata voted against and proposed raising the rate to around 1.5%. He argued that with underlying consumer price inflation having reached the bank’s 2% price stability target, the situation had moved into a new phase. In his view, the bank needs to speed up the pace of bringing its policy rate closer to the neutral rate, so that it can respond nimbly. His proposal was defeated by a majority vote.

The vote removes one of the main risks flagged ahead of the meeting. Two board members who opposed September’s rate hike had been seen as possible dissenters in favour of a cut. Analysts had warned that such a move could undercut a hawkish message and weaken the yen. Instead, the only dissent came from the hawkish side.

The board also voted unanimously to more than double the pace of its ETF sales. The bank began selling the funds in January this year at about 330 billion yen a year on a book value basis, equivalent to around 0.05% of market trading value. From January 2027, it will sell at about 0.1% of trading value, or roughly 860 billion yen a year on a book value basis. On a market value basis, that equates to about 2.5 trillion yen a year. The bank said the sales had proceeded smoothly without a major market impact, while trading in the stock market had expanded. It retained the option to adjust or suspend sales temporarily in response to market conditions. It left its sales of Japanese real estate investment trusts unchanged at about 5 billion yen a year.

Markets were pricing about an 80% chance of a hike in December going into the meeting. Attention now turns to the quarterly Outlook Report, which analysts expect to effectively declare that underlying inflation has reached 2%. Governor Kazuo Ueda’s press conference later in the afternoon will be watched for any signal on the timing of the next move.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.description:

Because a hold is fully priced, the market reaction will come from the language and the vote. A hawkish package would likely strengthen the yen and lift two-year yields. A dovish split could trigger renewed yen selling. Oil prices remain a background factor: Brent’s run of monthly gains strengthens the case for tighter policy because energy feeds directly into Japan’s import costs. Japanese bank stocks tend to benefit from signals of higher rates, while exporters could feel pressure from a firmer yen.

---

The Bank of Japan will almost certainly stand still today, so watch what it says, who votes against it and how Ueda chooses his words.

Summary:

  • The BoJ decision is due shortly, with no fixed release time; a hold at 1.25% is widely expected
  • Markets price about an 80% chance of a December hike
  • Analysts expect the Outlook Report to effectively declare that underlying inflation has reached 2%
  • Dissent risk runs both ways: two members could call for a cut, while another may push for a hike
  • Ueda’s press conference language will be key for December signals
  • Tokyo core CPI matched forecasts at 2.6%, output beat expectations and retail sales disappointed

The Bank of Japan is due to announce its policy decision shortly. The central bank is widely expected to keep its policy rate at 1.25%, and markets are focused on any signal that a hike is coming in December.

The decision has no fixed release time, but it typically lands around midday in Tokyo. A hold is almost fully expected, with traders pricing virtually no chance of a move at this meeting following hikes in June and September. Markets now see about an 80% chance of a December increase, up from earlier in the month, and a hawkish tone is widely anticipated.

Three elements will shape the market reaction. The first is the quarterly Outlook Report, in which analysts expect the board to effectively declare that underlying inflation has reached the bank’s 2% target. That would mark a shift from pushing inflation higher to keeping it stable. Policymakers may also nudge up their inflation forecasts as higher oil prices feed through to consumer prices.

The second is the vote. Two board members opposed the September hike and could dissent in favour of a cut. That would undercut a hawkish message and weigh on the yen. Another member may push in the opposite direction and propose a hike.

The third is Governor Kazuo Ueda’s press conference later in the afternoon. Any shift from saying rates are decided meeting by meeting toward language pointing to the next meeting would likely be read as a strong December signal.

The morning’s data gave policymakers a mixed picture. Core inflation in Tokyo, which excludes fresh food, came in at 2.6% in October, in line with forecasts and above target. Factory output rose more than expected in September, and manufacturers lifted their October production plans sharply, while retail sales fell short of expectations.

The yen has held steady near 157.8 per dollar ahead of the announcement. A clear 2% declaration, a firm Ueda and a hawkish dissent would likely support the currency and push short-dated Japanese government bond yields higher. A dovish split or a cautious tone could trim December expectations and weaken the yen. 

  Bank of Japan Governor Ueda press conference will follow at 0630 GMT.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: (Some good news!) Treasuries rally as AI selloff drives flight to safety, 10-year yield at one-month low
item.description:
Lower Treasury yields ease financing costs across the curve, offering some relief to rate-sensitive sectors and to the AI firms whose borrowing has worried investors. That makes the bond rally partly self-correcting for the very stress that triggered it. A softer dollar supports Asian currencies and commodities priced in dollars. Oil remains the main threat to the rally: with Brent heading for a fourth straight monthly gain, any escalation in the Iran conflict could quickly revive inflation fears and push yields back up. The BoJ decision later today is the next test, and a hawkish surprise could firm the yen against a softer dollar.

---

Stocks slammed:

  • Earnings bloodbath: Intel crashes over 22%, Amazon over 12%. What's coming next?

But ... at least Treasuries are bouncing!

The AI selloff finally gave bond investors something to cheer, though with oil still climbing and central banks still hawkish, the celebration may be brief.

Summary:

  • The US 10-year Treasury yield fell to around 4.90% and the 30-year to about 5.26%, both one-month lows
  • The rally was driven by safe-haven buying amid renewed selling in AI stocks after Alphabet, Amazon and Intel results
  • Strategists noted that AI concerns lowered yields and softened the dollar, unlike energy-driven risk-off episodes
  • The dollar index edged down to around 101.8 but is on track for a second straight monthly gain
  • The yen held near 157.8 ahead of the BoJ, with about an 80% chance of a December hike priced
  • ANZ’s Khoon Goh sees this week’s central bank pauses as temporary, with more hikes possible in 2027

US Treasuries rallied as a fresh wave of selling in artificial intelligence stocks sent investors in search of safety, Reuters reported on Friday. The rally pushed benchmark yields to their lowest levels in more than a month and weighed on the US dollar.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury note fell to around 4.90%, while the 30-year yield dropped to about 5.26%, both at more than one-month lows. Bond yields move inversely to prices, so the declines reflect strong buying of US government debt.

The rally was triggered by renewed concern over the cost of the AI boom. Results from Alphabet earlier in the week revived worries about AI spending and pulled broader stock markets lower. Disappointing results from Amazon and Intel after Thursday’s close added to the pressure. As equities sold off, safe-haven bonds became more attractive.

Strategists noted that the pattern differed from recent bouts of market stress. An energy-driven risk-off episode would typically lift the dollar and push yields higher. This time, one Singapore-based strategist said, the US-focused AI concerns came with lower Treasury yields and a softer or subdued dollar. That suggests investors are treating the AI selloff as a US growth and earnings risk rather than an inflation shock.

The lower yields weighed on the greenback. The dollar index, which tracks the US currency against a basket of major peers, edged down to around 101.8, although it remained on course for a second consecutive monthly gain.

Elsewhere in currency markets, the yen was steady near 157.8 per dollar ahead of the Bank of Japan’s policy decision. The central bank is expected to hold rates at 1.25% with a hawkish tone, and markets are pricing about an 80% chance of a hike in December. The euro was flat near $1.12 after touching its lowest level since May 2025 in the previous session. The Australian dollar held around $0.70, on track for a 1.2% gain in October.

The relief for bond markets may prove limited. The Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand all held rates steady this week, but have signalled their tightening cycles are not over, with energy prices near multi-month highs. Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at ANZ, described the current pauses as temporary. He said the risk heading into 2027 is that elevated inflation could bring even more hikes. Brent crude is on track for its fourth straight monthly gain, the longest run in more than two years.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Amazon and Intel results deepen worries over AI boom costs as tech, chip stocks slide
item.description:
The after-hours moves pointed to a weak start for Nasdaq futures in Asia, with semiconductor and AI infrastructure names most exposed in regional trade, including Asian chip and hardware suppliers. The funding angle may matter more than the earnings misses. Rising Big Tech debt issuance and pressure on leveraged AI cloud firms tie directly into concerns about tightening financial conditions and AI-related credit supply. If the selling deepens, investors may rotate toward the AI chip leaders that analysts see as less exposed to PC weakness, rather than out of the sector entirely.

---

Earlier:

  • Amazon Q3 operating profit beats estimates, but EPS misses and Q4 guidance looks soft. Share price drops.
  • Intel beats Q3 profit forecasts, but weak Q4 guidance and PC outlook weigh. Share price drops.
  • Intel shares tumble around 15%. The narrative is --> weak Q4 guidance overshadows Q3 profit beat
  • Earnings bloodbath: Intel crashes over 22%, Amazon over 12%. What's coming next?

---

The AI build-out is starting to send its bill to everyone, from Big Tech’s balance sheets to the shoppers paying more for their next laptop.

Summary:

  • Amazon fell about 7% after hours on a below-forecast holiday-quarter sales outlook
  • Intel dropped around 18% on weak PC demand and disclosed a $600 million revenue hit from an Israel factory explosion
  • AI cloud stocks CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren fell 6% to 7%, while HP and Dell sank about 8% and 7%
  • Alphabet and Meta burned cash in the September quarter, and Microsoft launched a $25 billion debt sale
  • Some analysts say Intel’s PC woes don’t necessarily signal trouble for AI-focused chipmakers
  • The semiconductor index is 21% below its June record despite a 60%-plus gain this year

Concern over the cost of the artificial intelligence boom intensified after the US market close on Thursday, Reuters reported. Results from Amazon and Intel suggested the race to build AI infrastructure is weighing not only on technology companies but also on consumers.

Amazon shares fell about 7% in after-hours trading after the company forecast holiday-quarter sales below Wall Street expectations. Reuters said that could signal growing pressure on consumers as inflation picks up. Intel dropped around 18% after flagging near-term weakness across the PC industry, where a shortage of memory chips has pushed up costs and price increases are squeezing demand for devices.

The selling spread well beyond the two companies. AI cloud providers CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren fell roughly 6% to 7% after hours. Alphabet, which had already closed nearly 13% lower following its own results, slipped a further 1.5%. PC makers HP and Dell dropped about 8% and 7%, respectively. In chips, AMD lost 4% and Broadcom 2%. A leveraged exchange-traded fund that offers three times the daily return of the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 9%.

Reuters highlighted a broader shift in how the largest technology firms are funding their spending. Heavy data centre investment has turned once debt-light companies into major borrowers. Alphabet and Meta both burned cash in the September quarter. Microsoft, the only one of the group not to do so, launched a $25 billion debt sale on Thursday. The biggest companies can sustain that spending, but investors have grown more cautious about smaller AI cloud firms borrowing heavily to meet large order backlogs.

Intel also disclosed that an explosion at a factory in Israel forced a two-week shutdown. It expects the incident to cost about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters.

Not everyone sees Intel’s PC troubles as a warning for the wider sector. Some analysts said weakness in personal computers does not necessarily signal problems for chipmakers more closely tied to AI. One trader attributed most of the after-hours chip selling to sentiment spilling over from Intel’s guidance.

The semiconductor index has risen more than 60% this year on shortages of AI-related chips and equipment, but tighter financing conditions have tested that rally over the past month. The index is down 13% from its October high and 21% below its June record.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chainalysis estimates $5.9B stolen in suspected Binance hack, nearly 4 times Bybit
item.description:
The Chainalysis estimate turns a containable loss into a balance-sheet question for Binance. A gap near $1 billion could be covered by SAFU, but one over $3 billion would test the exchange’s finances. That matters most for BNB, whose value is closely tied to Binance’s health. With deposits and withdrawals still frozen, any easing of selling pressure has to wait until Binance confirms the loss and explains how it will pay. Bitcoin and ether are more exposed to sentiment and liquidity at Binance than to the loss itself.

---

Earlier:

  • Binance halts deposits and withdrawals, pledges to cover all losses from suspected hack

... as it happened:

  1. Tether freezes $971M USDT amid suspected Binance hack as crypto sells off
  2. Binance appears hacked, CZ says, as Tether and Circle freeze $1.79B in stablecoins
  3. Binance pauses withdrawals after suspected $3B+ hack as Tether, Circle freeze $2.4B

Chainalysis puts the suspected Binance hack at $5.9 billion, which turns Binance’s promise to cover every loss from reassuring to expensive.

Summary:

  • Chainalysis estimates about $5.912 billion was stolen in the suspected Binance hack, according to CoinDesk.
  • That’s nearly four times the roughly $1.5 billion taken from Bybit in 2025, previously crypto’s largest theft.
  • Binance says $2.54 billion has been frozen, leaving about $3.4 billion potentially unrecovered on the Chainalysis figure.
  • The gap far exceeds Binance’s roughly $1 billion SAFU emergency fund, so most of any shortfall would fall on its balance sheet.
  • The estimate is well above CZ’s earlier suggestion that losses after freezes were slightly over $1 billion.
  • Binance has not confirmed a loss figure, and deposits and withdrawals remain suspended.

Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis estimates about $5.912 billion was stolen in the suspected hack of Binance, CoinDesk reported on Friday, 30 October. That’s nearly four times the 2025 Bybit theft, which previously held the record as crypto’s largest. The estimate is the first from a major analytics firm, and it sits at the top of the range of on-chain tallies circulating since Thursday evening.

The figure sharply raises the stakes for Binance’s pledge to cover all losses. The exchange has said verified frozen assets total $2.54 billion, most of it 1.567 billion USDT frozen by Tether and more than 800 million USDC frozen by Circle. Set against Chainalysis’s estimate, that leaves roughly $3.4 billion outside the freezes, though the gap could narrow if more funds are traced and blocked.

That is well beyond Binance’s Secure Asset Fund for Users, or SAFU, an emergency reserve of about $1 billion in bitcoin. If the Chainalysis estimate holds, most of any shortfall would have to come from Binance’s own balance sheet. The exchange has not said how it would fund the pledge. Frozen tokens are also not the same as recovered ones, since returning them through issuers or courts typically takes weeks.

The estimate also sits awkwardly with earlier signals. Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao had suggested losses after freezes may be slightly above $1 billion, while earlier on-chain reviews focused on about $3.3 billion leaving Binance’s Ethereum hot wallets. The Chainalysis number appears closer to wider tallies of around $5.6 billion that also include bitcoin and Tron outflows, which some analysts had cautioned were not yet tied to the attacker. Chainalysis has not published a breakdown, and Binance has not confirmed any loss figure.

Binance has suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it runs security checks and works with law enforcement, and it has promised a full post-mortem. It has given no date for reopening and has not said how the attacker gained access or who was responsible.

For scale, hackers stole about $1.5 billion from Bybit in February 2025, an attack the FBI attributed to North Korea. No agency or analytics firm has attributed the Binance incident to any group so far.

The next questions are whether Binance confirms or disputes the Chainalysis figure, how much more of the stolen funds can be frozen, and how the exchange will pay for losses that could run into billions of dollars. Those answers are likely to set the direction for BNB, Binance’s own token, which has borne the brunt of the selling since the outflows were first spotted.

For how the incident has unfolded so far, see our earlier reports on Binance pausing withdrawals after the suspected hack and its pledge to cover all losses.

If it’s in the billions, Binance’s finances come under scrutiny and BNB probably has further to fall.

Binance has stopped funds moving in or out and promised to cover every loss, but until it says how big the loss is, it’s a promise with no number attached.

Summary:

  • Binance suspended all deposits and withdrawals and pledged to cover all losses from the suspected hack, with co-CEO Yi He reported as announcing it.
  • Binance says verified frozen assets total $2.54 billion, including more than $2.37 billion from Tether and Circle.

  • There is no reopening date, loss figure or attribution yet, and a full post-mortem has been promised.

Binance has suspended all deposits and withdrawals and pledged to cover all losses from a suspected hack, as the exchange put the value of funds frozen so far at $2.54 billion. The move, announced on X shortly after 00:00 GMT on Friday, 30 October, widens an earlier partial pause on some networks. It also turns co-founder Changpeng Zhao’s personal expectation of full coverage into a company commitment.

Binance said the suspension would stay in place while its team runs security checks, freezes related funds and works with law enforcement. It promised a full post-mortem once its investigation is complete. ChainCatcher and PANews attributed the pledge to co-chief executive Yi He. The exchange gave no timetable for reopening and did not say how much it has lost, how the attacker gained access or who was responsible. It also paused trading on Binance Alpha, its platform for early-stage tokens.

In a separate post, Binance said verified frozen assets total $2.54 billion, with more tracing underway. Tether has frozen more than 1.567 billion USDT and Circle more than 800 million USDC, about $2.37 billion combined. That leaves roughly $170 million frozen by parties not yet named.

The size of the hole Binance has promised to fill remains unclear. Zhao has said losses may be slightly above $1 billion. FinanceFeeds tracked about $3.3 billion leaving Binance’s Ethereum hot wallets, which against the $2.54 billion frozen would leave a gap of about $760 million. A wider tally from Decrypt of at least $5.57 billion, which includes bitcoin and Tron outflows not yet tied to the attacker, would leave more than $3 billion uncovered. Frozen funds are also not the same as recovered funds, and getting them back through issuers or courts typically takes weeks.

Binance has a backstop. Its Secure Asset Fund for Users, or SAFU, an emergency reserve set up in 2018, holds about $1 billion in bitcoin. The exchange drew on it to cover a loss of 7,000 BTC in a 2019 hack. SAFU would cover the lower estimate, but anything near the higher figure would have to come from Binance’s own balance sheet.

Markets have drifted lower as the story has developed. Binance’s BNB token traded near $694 at about 00:15 GMT, down 8.6% over 24 hours, while bitcoin slipped to around $77,700, according to CoinGecko data cited by FinanceFeeds. Both are weaker than when withdrawals were first paused.

For Binance users, the immediate effect is that funds held on the exchange cannot be moved for now, even though the company says they are safe. Users should rely only on official Binance channels, as scams typically follow incidents like this. The next milestones are a confirmed loss figure, the post-mortem and a date for withdrawals to reopen. If losses are confirmed at the reported scale, the incident would surpass the $1.5 billion Bybit hack of February 2025 as the largest crypto theft on record.

Kyiv has quietly put its most effective economic weapon on hold until America votes, and Russia’s refineries get a breather while Ukraine’s power grid doesn’t.

  • Ukraine has paused strikes on Russian oil refineries, people familiar with the operations said
  • The informal pause began early last week and is expected to last until after the US midterms, possibly longer
  • Zelensky says forces have been more cautious but have not been ordered to stop

Ukraine has paused its drone strikes on Russian oil refineries following weeks of pressure from US President Donald Trump, according to a report in The Wall Street Journal (WSJ is gated) citing people with knowledge of the operations.

The unofficial pause began early last week and is expected to last at least until after the US midterm elections on Tuesday, and possibly further into November, the newspaper reported. Ukraine’s government has not announced any halt. Units carrying out long-range strikes were told in mid-October that the refinery campaign was effectively on hold once missions already under way were completed, according to two military officials cited in the report.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said this week that Ukrainian forces had been more cautious recently but had not been ordered to stop hitting refineries, and that drone units were striking other targets inside Russia. The last reported attack on Russian oil infrastructure was on 20 October, on a pumping station on the Druzhba pipeline.

The Journal reported that Trump has pressed Kyiv to stop the strikes, blaming them for high global fuel prices, which energy experts mostly attribute to the US-Iran war. Republican candidates are concerned fuel costs could hurt them in the midterms, and the administration has eased sanctions on Russian diesel. A US envoy repeated the demand for a pause at a meeting with Zelensky in Oslo on 20 October, according to US officials cited in the report.

The pause coincided with a dispute over Ukraine’s access to Starlink satellite internet, which was restricted in mid-October and fully restored on 24 October after Trump asked Elon Musk to lift the limits. US officials said the two issues were not linked, while some Ukrainian officials described heavy pressure to give Washington a win. European officials also advised Kyiv to take account of the political sensitivity of energy prices before the vote, the report said.

Zelensky has sought something in return for halting the strikes, with a mutual energy ceasefire with Russia his preferred option, but those proposals made little progress. Meanwhile, Russia has continued to escalate missile and drone attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and cities.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6548 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.description:

Stronger output and upbeat production plans support Japanese industrials and exporters. Softer retail sales could weigh on consumer-facing stocks if the weakness persists. ---

Japan’s factories are firing up while its shoppers are holding back, leaving the BoJ with one more mixed signal on a crowded morning.

Summary:

  • September industrial output rose 2.2% m/m, beating the 1.3% forecast, after a 2.4% drop in August
  • Output rose 1.9% y/y, slower than the prior 2.7%
  • Manufacturers expect output to rise 5.1% in October (previously forecast at 3.1%) and 0.8% in November
  • Retail sales fell 0.7% m/m, a second straight monthly decline
  • Retail sales rose 2.3% y/y, short of the 3.3% expected and down from 2.9%
  • The data land ahead of the BoJ decision, with a hold at 1.25% expected

Japan’s factory output rebounded more strongly than expected in September, but retail sales fell short of forecasts. That gives the Bank of Japan a mixed picture of the economy just hours before it announces its policy decision on Friday.

Industrial production rose 2.2% from August, well ahead of the median forecast for a 1.3% gain in a Reuters poll, and reversed much of the 2.4% drop recorded the previous month. Compared with a year earlier, output was up 1.9%, slower than the 2.7% annual pace in August.

The outlook from manufacturers was notably upbeat. Companies surveyed by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry expect seasonally adjusted output to jump 5.1% in October, a sharp upgrade from the 3.1% increase they had forecast a month earlier, before rising a further 0.8% in November. If those plans are met, factory activity would gain considerable momentum heading into the final weeks of the year, although manufacturers’ forecasts are often revised once actual production data are released.

Consumer spending was weaker. Retail sales fell 0.7% in September from August, a second consecutive monthly decline following a 1.2% drop in August. On an annual basis, sales rose 2.3%, short of the 3.3% expected and below the prior month’s 2.9% pace.

The split between strong production and softer spending is likely to feature in the central bank’s assessment. Policymakers are widely expected to keep the policy rate at 1.25% later on Friday, with markets focused on whether the board signals a hike in December. Robust output and a firm upgrade to production plans would support the view that the economy can withstand further tightening. Slowing retail sales, on the other hand, point to pressure on household budgets from higher prices.

The figures land on the same morning as Tokyo inflation data that showed core consumer prices in line with expectations. The BoJ’s quarterly Outlook Report, due later in the day, will show how policymakers weigh the latest signals on growth and inflation.

item.title: ANZ lifts year-end Brent forecast to $105 as tight physical market persists
item.description:
A $105 year-end call implies little relief for crude-importing economies, with Asian importers including Japan, India and South Korea most exposed through their currencies and trade balances. The asymmetry is notable. The bank’s upside risk sits about $15 above its base case, while its downside scenario needs both diplomatic and shipping breakthroughs, so the risk skew still favours higher prices. That supports energy equities and producer currencies such as the Canadian and Norwegian kroner exchange rates, and keeps upward pressure on headline inflation and bond yields across fuel-importing economies. Traders are likely to stay highly sensitive to headlines on Iran and on tanker traffic through Middle East shipping lanes.

---

  • RBA set for back-to-back hike after hot CPI, says Natixis’ Garcia Herrero

---

ANZ thinks oil stays expensive until the ships move freely again, and a peace deal on paper won’t be enough on its own.

Summary:

  • ANZ raised its 31 December Brent forecast to $105 a barrel from $95
  • It says physical constraints keeping the market tight are unlikely to ease before year end
  • A material escalation in the Iran conflict could push Brent to $120 or higher
  • A credible diplomatic breakthrough plus improved shipping could bring Brent back towards $90 to $95
  • The forecast was reported by Reuters on Friday

ANZ has raised its year-end forecast for Brent crude oil to $105 a barrel from $95, arguing that the physical constraints keeping the oil market tight are unlikely to ease before the end of December, Reuters reported on Friday.

The upgrade, which applies to the bank’s forecast for 31 December, marks a $10 increase. It reflects a judgement that supply-side pressures will persist for at least the next two months. Physical tightness refers to the balance between supply and demand for barrels available for delivery now, as distinct from futures pricing driven by positioning or sentiment.

The bank set out a wide range of outcomes around its base case, with the Iran conflict the main swing factor. According to ANZ, a material escalation in the conflict would create the risk of Brent rising to $120 a barrel or higher. In the other direction, a credible diplomatic breakthrough in the Middle East, combined with a material improvement in shipping conditions, could see prices move back towards $90 to $95 a barrel.

The emphasis on shipping is notable. ANZ’s downside scenario requires both a diplomatic solution and a clear recovery in shipping, which suggests the bank sees disruption to tanker routes as a key source of the current tightness. A ceasefire or political agreement on its own may not be enough to bring prices down quickly if vessels still face restrictions or elevated risks.

The revision adds to the debate over how high energy costs will feed into inflation and interest rate decisions worldwide. Central banks from Australia to Japan and Europe have pointed to fuel prices as a key driver of recent inflation, and a sustained Brent price above $100 would keep that pressure in place into the new year.

For now, ANZ’s central view is that oil will remain elevated through year end, with the balance of risks set largely by events in the Middle East.

item.title: Binance pauses withdrawals after suspected $3B+ hack as Tether, Circle freeze $2.4B
item.description:
The market has largely moved past the initial shock. BNB has bounced off its low and bitcoin is steady near $78,800, which suggests traders see the freezes and CZ’s pledge as limiting the damage to Binance itself. The next risk is supply. The attacker holds more than $1 billion in ether and has already been selling smaller tokens on decentralised exchanges, so large ETH sales could weigh on ether’s price. Partial withdrawal pauses at the world’s biggest exchange also tighten liquidity before Friday’s monthly options expiry on Deribit at 08:00 GMT.

---

Earlier:

  • Binance appears hacked, CZ says, as Tether and Circle freeze $1.79B in stablecoins
  • Tether freezes $971M USDT amid suspected Binance hack as crypto sells off

--- Binance has stopped part of its withdrawals and stablecoin issuers have locked up $2.4 billion, but the ether that got away keeps this suspected hack on course to be crypto’s largest.

Summary:

  • Binance temporarily paused withdrawals on multiple networks after more than $3 billion was drained from its Ethereum hot wallets on 29 October.
  • Tether froze more than 1.567 billion USDT and Circle more than 800 million USDC, about $2.4 billion in total. More than $1 billion, mostly ether, remains unfrozen.
  • Binance says user funds are completely safe but hasn’t called it a hack or given a loss figure. CZ says it looks like a hack and expects losses to be covered.
  • The attacker used EIP-7702, an Ethereum feature that lets a wallet run contract code, from an address funded through Tornado Cash.
  • BNB fell to about $692 before recovering to around $704. Bitcoin is near $78,800.
  • If confirmed, the theft would more than double Bybit’s record $1.5 billion hack in 2025.

Binance has paused withdrawals on several networks after more than $3 billion was drained from its Ethereum hot wallets late on Thursday, 29 October, in what co-founder Changpeng Zhao says looks like a hack. Tether and Circle have together frozen about $2.4 billion in stablecoins, but more than $1 billion, mostly ether, remains out of reach.

Binance spokesperson Ross O’Leary told TechCrunch the exchange had temporarily suspended withdrawals on multiple networks as a precaution. Binance has said user funds are completely safe and that withdrawals will resume once the security issue is fully resolved. It has not used the word hack, given a loss figure or explained how the funds left. An early version of its statement on X said it had not confirmed any impact on user funds, and it was later edited to say funds were safe, FinanceFeeds reported.

Zhao, who stepped down as chief executive in 2023 but remains Binance’s largest shareholder, said user funds are safe and that he expects them to be fully covered. Tech-ish reported that he later put the loss after freezes at about $1 billion, possibly a little higher, and said Binance would cover it.

The freezes are larger than first reported. Tether chief executive Paolo Ardoino said more than 1.567 billion USDT had been frozen, up from the roughly $971 million Zhao cited earlier. Circle said it froze more than 800 million USDC in coordination with law enforcement. About 700 million USDT left the receiving address before Tether’s blacklist took effect, and much of it was swapped into ether, according to Tech-ish.

On-chain data points to an outside attacker. A wallet labelled Binance 14 was linked to a smart contract set up by an address funded through Tornado Cash, a crypto mixing service. The attacker used EIP-7702, an Ethereum feature that lets an ordinary wallet run contract code. Minutes later, a single transaction moved about 167,000 ETH, roughly 1.6 billion USDT and 62 other tokens to a new address. The attacker has since been selling tokens the stablecoin issuers cannot freeze, including UNI and PEPE, on decentralised exchanges. Some tallies circulating on X put total outflows above $5 billion, but those include bitcoin and Tron movements not yet tied to the attacker.

Crypto markets steadied after the initial drop. BNB, Binance’s own token used for trading-fee discounts and fees on its affiliated BNB Chain, fell from about $739 to a low near $692 before recovering to about $704 by 22:15 GMT, CryptoTicker data showed. Bitcoin was near $78,800 and ether around $2,265. About $628 million in leveraged positions were liquidated within an hour, mostly longs.

If confirmed, the Ethereum transfers alone would more than double the $1.5 billion stolen from Bybit in February 2025, the largest crypto theft on record, which the FBI attributed to North Korea. Traders will watch for a formal Binance loss figure and reimbursement plan, whether the attacker dumps its ether on the market, and how quickly withdrawals reopen. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia in talks to guarantee Nscale debt tied to $45 billion Anthropic compute deal
item.description:
For Nvidia shares, the trade-off is between locking in demand for its next-generation chips and taking on contingent credit risk tied to a pre-IPO company. That balance may draw closer scrutiny of the off-balance-sheet exposure Nvidia reports in future filings. The report also matters for AI credit more broadly. Guarantees from a highly rated supplier could narrow the spreads that smaller data centre developers pay to borrow, easing one of the funding strains markets have been worried about. Nscale’s planned IPO could benefit from the added backing, though investors are likely to ask how much of its revenue depends on financing from its own supplier.

---

---

Nvidia already sells the chips and owns a stake in the landlord. Now it may co-sign the mortgage too.

Summary:

  • Nvidia is reportedly in talks to provide credit guarantees for billions of dollars of Nscale debt
  • The debt would fund a 460MW data centre that Anthropic plans to use, linked to a deal worth about $45 billion
  • The capacity sits at Nscale’s Monarch campus in West Virginia and uses Nvidia’s Vera Rubin chips
  • No deal has been signed, and the terms could change
  • Nscale filed for a US IPO in September, targeting a valuation of about $30 billion, with Nvidia among its investors
  • The talks revive concerns about circular financing in the AI build-out

Nvidia is in talks to provide credit guarantees covering billions of dollars of debt for Nscale, a young AI cloud provider, according to a report by The Information. The guarantees would help fund a data centre that Anthropic plans to use under a deal worth about $45 billion.

The guarantees would support Nscale’s borrowing to develop a 460-megawatt facility. The size of the credit support has not been disclosed, nothing has been signed and the terms could still change, according to people familiar with the discussions cited in the report.

The facility is linked to a computing agreement first reported by Bloomberg earlier this month. Under it, Anthropic was in late-stage talks to buy about $45 billion of capacity from Nscale. The capacity would come from a second building at Nscale’s Monarch campus in West Virginia, running on Nvidia’s Vera Rubin chips. Anthropic took over the site after Microsoft withdrew from a preliminary letter of intent it signed in March. Filings tied to Nscale’s planned listing show existing Anthropic infrastructure commitments of close to $45 billion.

Nscale filed publicly for a US initial public offering in September, targeting a valuation of about $30 billion. It recently closed a pre-IPO funding round of about $3.4 billion led by Third Point, with Nvidia among the investors.

If agreed, the guarantees would give Nvidia three roles in the same deal chain: chip supplier, equity investor in the cloud provider and backer of its debt. That structure has drawn criticism before. In September, Anthropic signed a $35 billion compute deal with Lambda, another Nvidia-backed cloud provider, and critics argued that Nvidia was effectively underwriting demand for its own chips. Nvidia’s finance chief has said the company sees those arrangements differently.

Supporters of these deals argue that guarantees from a cash-rich supplier lower borrowing costs for capital-hungry cloud builders and speed up capacity that customers have already committed to use. Sceptics counter that such guarantees tie Nvidia’s balance sheet more closely to the fortunes of smaller, highly leveraged firms, and that some revenue may depend on financing Nvidia itself helps provide.

The report lands as investors focus on how the AI build-out is being funded. Morgan Stanley has flagged rising AI-related debt issuance and wider credit spreads on data centre bonds as one of the main pressures on equities in the coming weeks. How the Nscale financing is structured, and how much risk Nvidia takes on, is likely to feed that debate.

There’s also a possible two-stage dollar trade, though this is editorial interpretation rather than Morgan Stanley’s view. A final risk-off shock could lift the US dollar on safe-haven demand. If that stress pushes the Fed toward easing, it could also mark a peak in dollar strength. Higher energy prices tied to the Iran conflict remain a risk to the timeline, since they add to the tightening pressure Wilson describes.

---

Morgan Stanley thinks the stock correction has one more leg down in it, and that the stress which delivers it may also bring the Fed to the rescue.

Summary:

  • Wilson says the equity correction that began in June is in its final stages
  • He sees tactical S&P 500 downside to 7,100-7,200, then a year-end target of 8,000
  • AI concerns are expected to peak in three to four weeks as debt supply is absorbed, and chips could fall another 10% to 15%
  • Morgan Stanley sees the midterms as a hurdle that markets typically benefit from clearing
  • Wilson calls liquidity the key catalyst: financial conditions are near 2018 levels and close to 2022 severity, which risks forcing a Fed reversal
  • Chips, financials, consumer cyclicals and autos are seen leading any recovery

Morgan Stanley’s Mike Wilson believes the US equity correction that began in June is in its final stages. He expects markets may need one last sell-off before a sustained recovery, with three catalysts set to determine when the bottom arrives.

Wilson, the bank’s chief US equity strategist, sees tactical downside for the S&P 500 to between 7,100 and 7,200, slightly below its 200-day moving average, before a rebound towards his year-end target of 8,000. He argues that much of the damage has already been done beneath the surface of the headline index. About 60% of Russell 3000 stocks are down more than 20% since the correction began, and in semiconductors the figure is 96%.

The first catalyst is artificial intelligence. Morgan Stanley expects investor concerns over AI to peak over the next three to four weeks as markets absorb a sharp increase in related debt issuance. Those concerns include returns on capital, funding needs, widening credit spreads on data centre bonds and local opposition to new facilities. The bank’s strategists said semiconductors could fall a further 10% to 15% before finding support around mid-November.

The second is the US midterm elections. Morgan Stanley sees the vote as a hurdle that markets benefit from clearing, rather than a lasting threat. It notes that the S&P 500 has historically gained about 17% on average in the 12 months after a midterm election.

Wilson regards the third catalyst, liquidity, as the most important. The Federal Reserve has resumed rate increases and roughly halved the pace of its balance sheet growth, while higher energy prices add further pressure. In Wilson’s view, markets are effectively tightening financial conditions on the Fed’s behalf, and those conditions have now tightened to a degree comparable with 2018 and nearly as severe as 2022. That could slow growth and help bring inflation down. He warned, however, that it may also generate enough financial stress to force the Fed to reverse course before inflation is fully contained.

Wilson sees opportunities as these catalysts resolve. Sentiment is neutral and third-quarter earnings growth is running near 27%. He expects early-cycle groups that have lagged, including chips, financials, consumer cyclicals and autos, to lead any recovery, with semiconductors offering the most rebound potential. The main risk to the view is timing: a slower resolution of any catalyst would push the expected bottom further out. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA set for back-to-back hike after hot CPI, says Natixis’ Garcia Herrero
item.description:
A back-to-back hike would extend the Australian dollar’s rate advantage and keep front-end yields elevated, while any hint that November is the last move could trigger a pullback in both. Fuel is the key transmission channel, so oil prices remain central to the outlook: further crude gains would deepen the pass-through into services and strengthen calls for more tightening. Australian equities, particularly rate-sensitive sectors such as property and consumer discretionary, face added pressure if markets begin to price a longer hiking path.

---

Earlier:

  • ING lifts AUD/USD target to 0.71 as it backs a 25bp RBA hike next week

---

Fuel is no longer just a petrol-station problem for Australia’s inflation, and Natixis expects the RBA to respond again next week.

Summary:

  • September CPI rose about 0.8% m/m and 4.3% y/y, above forecasts of 0.7% and 4.2%
  • Energy added about 0.3 points to the monthly rise, while travel contributed around 0.43 points, its most since December 2025
  • Garcia Herrero sees the energy shock passing through to the broader basket
  • The Q3 trimmed mean edged up to about 3.7%, diverging from the RBA’s August forecast of a peak in Q2
  • Hauser and Bullock comments reinforce the RBA’s low tolerance for persistent inflation
  • Natixis expects a back-to-back hike on 3 November, with later decisions highly data dependent

Australia’s September inflation data delivered a sharp upside surprise that is likely to push the Reserve Bank of Australia into a back-to-back rate hike at its meeting on Tuesday, 3 November. That is the view of Alicia Garcia Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at Natixis and one of the more closely followed analysts of the RBA.

Headline consumer prices rose about 0.8% in September from August and around 4.3% from a year earlier, both ahead of consensus forecasts of 0.7% and 4.2%. Garcia Herrero said the print surprised the market as well as the central bank.

The detail is what concerns her most. Energy added roughly a third of a percentage point to the monthly increase, but travel was the single largest driver, contributing around 0.43 percentage points, its biggest contribution since December 2025. Travel prices are closely tied to fuel costs, so Garcia Herrero said the data suggest the energy shock has begun to filter through to the wider basket of goods and services. She described this as a warning sign for policymakers.

Underlying inflation is also moving away from the path the RBA expected. The trimmed mean, the central bank’s preferred core measure, rose to about 3.7% year on year in the third quarter, edging up from the second quarter. In August, the RBA had projected that the trimmed mean would peak in the second quarter and ease back towards 3.3% by the end of 2026. The latest reading widens the gap between that forecast and the actual inflation path.

Garcia Herrero linked the data to recent comments from RBA officials. Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser recently described the inflation outlook as having deteriorated materially. Governor Michele Bullock told a parliamentary hearing this week that the central bank will not tolerate inflation remaining persistently high. Against that backdrop, Garcia Herrero expects the RBA to favour another hike next week.

Beyond November, she expects policy to become more finely balanced. The RBA is likely to keep a hawkish tone while inflation remains elevated. However, signs of an easing labour market and slowing household spending under higher interest rates mean subsequent decisions are likely to be highly data dependent. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.description:
Front-end Australian yields look most exposed to next week’s decision, with roughly 5bp of hike pricing still to close if the RBA moves. A hold would likely hit the Australian dollar hard, given how much of its October strength rests on rate expectations. Oil is a key driver: further gains in crude would add to fuel-led inflation and reinforce the tightening bias, while a sustained pullback could ease pressure on the RBA. The Fed’s stance remains the main external constraint on AUD/USD.

---

---

ING likes the Aussie’s yield and expects the RBA to add to it next week, but sees the Fed standing between AUD/USD and 0.72.

Summary:

  • ING raised its short-term AUD/USD target to 0.71, but doesn’t expect a return to 0.72 this quarter
  • It says the Australian dollar offers the best volatility-adjusted short-term carry in G10
  • ING expects a 25bp RBA hike on 3 November, taking the cash rate to 4.85%, against about 20bp priced
  • Headline CPI hit 4.3% y/y in September, driven almost entirely by fuel-related transport costs
  • Goods and services inflation are both above 4%, and core inflation accelerated
  • A hawkish Fed is expected to keep supporting the US dollar, limiting AUD gains

ING has raised its short-term forecast for the Australian dollar to 0.71 against the US dollar, citing the currency’s strong October and its attractive yield advantage. The bank does not expect AUD/USD to climb back to 0.72 this quarter, however, as a hawkish Federal Reserve keeps supporting the greenback.

The upgrade rests on ING’s view that the Reserve Bank of Australia will raise its cash rate by 25 basis points at its 3 November meeting, rather than waiting until December. That would lift the cash rate to 4.85%. The bank had previously pencilled in a hike at some point in the fourth quarter, and now sees the latest inflation data as strong enough to bring the move forward. Markets are pricing around 20 basis points of tightening for next week, slightly short of a full hike.

ING said AUD/USD is driven mainly by short-term interest rate differentials. It added that the Australian dollar currently offers the best short-term carry in the G10 once volatility is taken into account. Carry refers to the return investors earn from holding a higher-yielding currency, and a further RBA hike would widen that advantage.

The inflation backdrop supports the case. Headline consumer prices rose 4.3% from a year earlier in September, with inflation picking up by about 90 basis points between July and September, based on the latest monthly figures and the third-quarter report. Almost all of that increase came from transport costs, largely reflecting higher fuel prices. ING noted that goods and services inflation are both now running above 4%, a sign that energy costs are spreading more widely through the economy. Core inflation also accelerated on both annual and quarterly measures. The trimmed mean rose to 3.7%, above forecasts and well above the RBA’s target band.

ING concluded that underlying inflation is not on a sustained downward path, weakening any argument for a pause. At its last meeting, the RBA raised rates unanimously and signalled it was prepared to accept some softening in the labour market to bring inflation back to target.

The main limit on further Australian dollar gains lies outside Australia. With the Fed also leaning hawkish, ING expects the US dollar to remain supported, capping the upside for AUD/USD in the near term even if the RBA delivers next week.
